title: Karisma Kapoor Is Playing a Broken, Alcoholic Detective in Kolkata. The Show Is Uneven. She Is Not.
excerpt: Brown on ZEE5 delivers a flawed neo-noir thriller and a career-best performance from an actress the industry had quietly stopped calling.
body:
The opening shot tells you everything. **Karisma Kapoor** stands at a crime scene in Kolkata, her silhouette battered by the kind of shadows that only exist in cities with crumbling colonial architecture and too many secrets. She is not glamorous. She is not charming. She is not playing anyone you would invite to a party. And she has never been better.

<youtube>https://youtube.com/watch?v=prdjv5IWPWY</youtube>

**Brown**, now streaming on **ZEE5**, is a seven-episode neo-noir crime thriller directed by **Abhinay Deo** (of **Delhi Belly** fame) and adapted from **Abheek Barua's novel City of Death**. Kapoor plays **Rita Brown**, a suspended police officer with an alcohol dependency, a dead husband, a lost pregnancy, and the kind of self-destructive streak that makes even her colleagues uncomfortable. When a young woman named Ahana is found murdered in her home, Rita is pulled back into homicide work — and into a conspiracy that reaches into Kolkata's political establishment.

On paper, this is a been-there-watched-that premise. On screen, it is something more complicated: a show whose writing cannot quite keep pace with its lead performance.

> "This was very enriching. I had to go into a very dark place for this role. It's the most complex character I've ever played." — Karisma Kapoor

https://www.instagram.com/p/DZKicisjT98/

The reviews have been sharply divided on the series — ratings ranging from 2 to 3.5 out of 5 — but the consensus on Karisma is remarkably unified. Across every major publication, critics have called her work as Rita Brown the standout element: "the finest performance in years," "she alone is almost worth the whole ordeal," "an actor operating at a frequency the material struggles to match." When every critic agrees on one thing in an otherwise contentious review landscape, that thing is probably real.

What makes the performance work is how thoroughly Karisma has abandoned vanity. Rita Brown does not have a single scene where she looks put-together. Her hair is a mess. Her eyes are glassy. She drinks in her car, at crime scenes, in interrogation rooms. The woman who defined elegance in **Dil To Pagal Hai** and collected two **National Awards** before stepping away from the industry in 2003 is now playing someone who would not survive a wellness check. It is a transformation that goes beyond physical — there is a heaviness to how Karisma occupies Rita's body, a weariness that feels lived-in rather than performed.

The supporting cast adds texture. **Jisshu Sengupta** plays the psychiatrist with his trademark Bengali cool. **Surya Sharma** grounds the procedural sequences as Rita's partner. **Helen Khan** appears as a neighbour. And **Soni Razdan** brings maternal gravity as Rita's mother. Kolkata itself is shot as a character — rain-slicked alleys, yellow cabs, decaying mansions that hold the city's real wealth and its real rot.

Where Brown falters is in its construction. The series introduces too many subplots and secondary characters that dilute the central mystery. Entire episodes detour into Ahana's friendships, romantic entanglements, and social circles without adding momentum. The pacing can be glacial — and not in the deliberate, tension-building way the best noir achieves. The trailer, unfortunately, gave away enough of the plot architecture that several reveals land with diminished impact. Deo's direction captures the atmosphere but struggles to maintain the structural discipline that a seven-episode mystery demands.

**For diaspora audiences**, Brown is streaming on ZEE5, which is available globally. If you grew up watching Karisma Kapoor in the 1990s — if **Raja Hindustani** or **Fiza** or **Zubeida** meant something to your adolescence — this is the role that proves she has been waiting for material worthy of her range, not the other way around. She chose to step away from films after marriage. She returned on her own terms with **Mentalhood** in 2020. Now, at a moment when Bollywood is finally writing women as more than decoration, she has delivered the kind of performance that reminds you why she was the actress everyone else was measured against.

Brown is an imperfect show built around a perfect piece of acting. Watch it for the detective. Stay for the actress who decided, after two decades of being underestimated, that she had something left to prove.
